meta.title: Who really said "When something is important enough, you do it even if the odds are not in your favor"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine Elon Musk. He said it on CBS's 60 Minutes (aired March 18, 2012) when Scott Pelley asked why he started SpaceX against the odds.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When something is important enough, you do it even if the odds are not in your favor'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Elon Musk. CBS's transcript of the 2012 60 Minutes segment on SpaceX shows him saying it, in reply to Scott Pelley's question "Why even begin?"

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: b. 1971 · Founder and CEO of SpaceX
answer.sourceLine: Musk said it on CBS’s 60 Minutes, in the segment “SpaceX” with correspondent Scott Pelley, which aired March 18, 2012. CBS News’s own transcript confirms the exact wording, given in reply to Pelley’s question “Why even begin?”

source.heading: The broadcast

docMeta.dd: Scott Pelley, correspondent; Harry Radliffe, producer
CBS News, “SpaceX: Entrepreneur’s race to space,” June 20, 2012

source.excerpt: Elon Musk: The odds of me coming into the rocket business, not knowing anything about rockets, not having ever built anything, I mean, I would have to be insane if I thought the odds are in my favor. Scott Pelley: Why even begin? Elon Musk: When something is important enough you do it even if the odds are not in your favor. Scott Pelley: How much of your personal fortune have you poured into this? Elon Musk: $100 million.

source.excerptNote: CBS’s transcript has no comma after “enough.” The comma in the popular version is the only difference.

author.bio: Elon Musk is the founder and chief executive of SpaceX and the chief executive of Tesla. In 2012 60 Minutes described him as the Internet entrepreneur “of PayPal and Tesla Motors fame” for whom SpaceX was a first venture in aerospace. He told Scott Pelley he had put $100 million of his own fortune into the company.

misattribution.heading: Genuine, but often passed around without context
misattribution.intro: This one is not misattributed. It usually circulates on quote sites and in listicles with no date or source, though, and it gets confused with the remark Musk made just before it.

items.why: The line is widely shared with no broadcast or date. Wikiquote’s Talk:Elon Musk ↗ page still includes it in a list of “further unsourced quotes” whose only citation is an Inc.com listicle. The main Wikiquote article ↗ now cites the 2012 60 Minutes broadcast for it.

items.who: “I would have to be insane if I thought the odds were in my favor”
items.why: This is a separate sentence that Musk said just before, in the same exchange. CBS’s own 2020 article ↗ uses it, with “were,” as its headline. The 2012 transcript ↗ has “the odds are in my favor.”

misattribution.truthLine: Musk really did say it, in the March 18, 2012 60 Minutes segment “SpaceX,” as recorded in CBS News’s transcript ↗.

context.heading: Why he said it
lead: Scott Pelley had just heard Musk admit he would “have to be insane” to think the odds favored a newcomer who knew nothing about rockets. So Pelley asked, “Why even begin?” Musk’s answer was this line, and he then said he had put $100 million of his own fortune into SpaceX.

The same segment tells how the first three flights of SpaceX’s Falcon 1 rocket failed to reach orbit. Musk told Pelley that if the fourth launch hadn’t worked, “that would have been it,” because the company lacked the resources to mount a fifth.

sourcesVerified.claim: CBS transcript of the 60 Minutes segment 'SpaceX' (aired March 18, 2012, rebroadcast June 3, 2012; Scott Pelley correspondent, Harry Radliffe producer; page dated June 20, 2012) contains 'Scott Pelley: Why even begin? Elon Musk: When something is important enough you do it even if the odds are not in your favor.' It also contains the preceding 'insane... odds are in my favor' line, the $100 million, the three failed Falcon 1 flights and the fourth-launch remarks.

Wikiquote's Elon Musk article lists 'When something is important enough, you do it even if the odds are not in your favor.' under ===2012===, cited to the 18 March 2012 60 Minutes broadcast; it gives Musk's birth date as 28 June 1971.
